videos.script: Four things sit inside every computer you will ever open, and this lesson is what each one does when it is working and what it looks like when it is not. {{four}} The processor does the arithmetic. Memory is the desk it works on. Storage is the filing cabinet beside the desk. And the motherboard is the wiring between the three — not a fourth worker, but the building they are in. {{parts}} That picture is enough to answer the question people actually arrive with, which is why a machine feels slow. Slow is never a property of the computer. It is a property of whichever of the four is being waited on, and the four are not waited on at anything like the same speed. {{wait}} A processor reads something it is already holding in about a nanosecond. It reads memory in about a hundred. It reads a solid-state drive in about a hundred thousand. A spinning disk is ten million. Those are not four points on a scale — they are four different worlds, and almost every piece of advice you have been given about making a computer faster is really about not falling into the next world down. {{hierarchy}} So we take them one at a time, and finish somewhere useful: reading a specification off a shop page and saying which of the four it is going to disappoint.
